tasks.task_description: Requirement 1: Construct a mathematical model to identify the best 3-dimensional geometric shape for a sandcastle foundation that lasts the longest under waves and tides, given the same beach, sand type, sand volume, and water-to-sand proportion. The model must rank candidate shapes by survival time against a concrete, citable wave-and-tide scenario.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) The foundation has fixed volume V0 = 0.5 m³ and sits at a fixed distance from the mean waterline. (2) Wave forcing: significant wave height H = 1 m, period T = 8 s (Item 2: Masselink & Short 2005, fair-to-moderate conditions); swash reach above the mean waterline is 1 m. (3) Tidal range = 1.5 m (micro-to-meso-tidal). (4) The wet-sand cohesion follows the capillary-bond model C(w) = C0·exp(−((w−w*)/σ)²), with w* = 1% (Item 1: Pakpour et al. 2012), C0 = 50 Pa, σ = 0.05. (5) Erosion is time-varying: the erosion rate is proportional to the wave energy flux divided by the current cohesion C(t), which decays as cumulative pore water rises from repeated swash (expert exchange 3). (6) Failure is evaluated on the evolving strength: collapse when C(t) falls below a critical cohesion C_crit = 5 Pa (10% of peak); washout (swash reaching the top of the mound) is a secondary endpoint. (7) A separate tidal-submergence erosion term K_sub/C(t) is added when the tide exceeds the mound height. Method: semi-implicit time integration with dt = 1 s over a 1-hour horizon, tracking height H(t), cumulative moisture w(t), and cohesion C(t) for each shape. This approach is sound because it embeds the two physically dominant, underspecified choices identified by the expert (failure criterion and erosion magnitude) as explicit parameters, sweeps them across plausible ranges, and uses the literature-anchored cohesion peak to govern the time-varying strength.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cohesion model: C(w) = C0·exp(−((w−w*)/σ)²) Pa, with C0 = 50 Pa, w* = 0.01, σ = 0.05. Wave energy flux: P = ρ_w·g²·H²/(8T) W/m², ρ_w = 1025 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². For H = 1 m, T = 8 s, P ≈ 157 W/m². Shape catalog (all at V0 = 0.5 m³): (a) half-cylinder, squat L = 2r, V = πr³, H0 = r, A_base = 4r², wetted perimeter = 4r; (b) cone, h = r, V = πr³/3, H0 = r, A_base = πr², wetted perimeter = 2πr; (c) rectangular block, L = W = 2H, V = 4H³, H0 = (V0/4)^(1/3), A_base = 4H0², wetted perimeter = 8H0; (d) hemisphere, V = (2/3)πr³, H0 = r, A_base = πr², wetted perimeter = 2πr. Dynamics per timestep dt: (i) Tidal elevation: z_tide(t) = (R/2)(1 + sin(2πt/T_tide)), R = 1.5 m, T_tide = 12.42 h. (ii) Swash maximum: z_swash = z_tide + s, s = 1 m. (iii) Moisture update: dw/dt = K_sat/T_wave (if wave reaches base) + r_drainage, K_sat = 0.005 (liquid fraction per strike), drainage = 0.001/h. (iv) Cohesion: C(t) = C(w(t)). (v) Wave erosion: dH/dt|wave = K_wave·P·(p_wet·H·f_wet)/(C(t)·A_base·ρ_sand·g), where p_wet is wetted perimeter, f_wet = 0.5 (fraction of perimeter wetted), ρ_sand = 1600 kg/m³. (vi) Submergence erosion: dH/dt|sub = K_sub/C(t) if z_tide > H, else 0, K_sub = 0.1 m/s at C = 1 Pa. (vii) Failure: C(t) < C_crit = 5 Pa (structural collapse) or H ≤ 0.05·H0 (washout). Survival time T_surv is the time to first failure. Parameters: K_wave = 1.0 (base), swept 0.1–5.0; K_sat = 0.005, swept 0.001–0.05; H_wave = 1.0 m, swept 0.5–2.0 m; tide_range = 1.5 m, swept 0.5–4.0 m.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case (K_wave = 1.0, K_sat = 0.005, H_wave = 1 m, tide = 1.5 m): survival times are cone 0.035 h (127 s), half-cylinder 0.033 h, hemisphere 0.032 h, block 0.029 h. The cone (tall, pointed, small base area relative to height) ranks first in the base case and in the majority of the 60-case parameter sweep; the half-cylinder takes first place when K_sat is high (≥ 0.01) or K_wave is low (≤ 0.1), because its larger base area dilutes the per-area erosion rate when cohesion decay is fast. The ranking is therefore not a single robust winner: it depends on the relative magnitudes of the wave-erosion and moisture-saturation rates. Limitations: (1) The absolute survival times (~2 min) are short because the model is conservative — K_wave = 1.0 and C0 = 50 Pa are upper-bound values; at K_wave = 0.1, cone survival extends to 139 s. (2) The model treats the foundation as a 1-D column with uniform height erosion; it does not resolve local scour at the base or slumping of the upper mass, which would shorten survival for tall shapes. (3) The cohesion decay is driven by a constant saturation rate K_sat; in reality, drainage and evaporation are spatially non-uniform. (4) The shape catalog is discrete; a continuous profile z(x) optimised by calculus of variations would likely favour a shape with a large base area and a tapered top (close to the cone or hemisphere family). The model's central finding — that a shape with a small base area and tall profile (cone) is favoured when wave erosion dominates, while a shape with a large base area (half-cylinder) is favoured when cohesion decay dominates — is robust to the parameter sweeps tested.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2: Determine the optimal sand-to-water mixture proportion for the castle foundation, using no other additives or materials.
tasks.task_analysis: The mixture proportion is governed by the capillary-cohesion model C(w) = C0·exp(−((w−w*)/σ)²), where w is the liquid volume fraction. Item 1 (Pakpour et al., Scientific Reports 4, 549, 2012) establishes that wet-sand elastic modulus and cohesive strength peak at w* ≈ 1% (liquid volume relative to the dry sand + liquid mixture), with a broadly castable range of 0.5–15% by volume. The model uses this peak as the backbone of the strength-vs-moisture curve. The optimisation is to maximise C(w) over w ∈ [0, 0.20], which is a single-peaked unimodal function; the maximum occurs at w = w* = 0.01. The sand-to-water ratio by volume is (1−w*):w* = 0.99:0.01 = 99:1. By weight, using ρ_sand = 1600 kg/m³ and ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, the ratio is 1600×0.99 : 1000×0.01 = 1584:10 = 158:1.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Strength function: C(w) = C0·exp(−((w−w*)/σ)²) Pa, C0 = 50 Pa, w* = 0.01, σ = 0.05. Maxima: dC/dw = 0 → w = w* = 0.01. C(0.01) = 50 Pa (peak). Castling range (C > 0.05·C_peak): w ∈ [0.001, 0.096], i.e. 0.1%–9.6% by volume, consistent with the literature range of 0.5%–15%. Sand-to-water ratio at optimum: by volume = (1−0.01)/0.01 = 99:1; by weight = 1600×0.99/(1000×0.01) = 158:1. Practical recipe: for every 100 mL of dry sand, add approximately 1 mL of water (by volume), or for every 158 g of dry sand, add 1 g of water (by weight). The sand should be mixed to a 'dry-sand-that-holds-its-shape' consistency — wet enough that capillary bridges form between grains, but not so wet that the water films merge into a lubricating layer.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The optimal proportion is approximately 99 parts sand to 1 part water by volume (158:1 by weight), corresponding to a liquid volume fraction of 1%. This is the point of maximum capillary cohesion and therefore maximum resistance to wave and tidal erosion. The strength curve is sharply peaked: at 5% moisture, cohesion is 26 Pa (53% of peak); at 10%, it is 2 Pa (4% of peak). This means the mixture is tolerant of small errors in the 0.5–2% range but degrades rapidly above 5%. The model's bias: the Gaussian form of C(w) is a fitting approximation to the true capillary-bond strength curve, which is believed to be asymmetric (a steeper decline above the optimum than below it). The 1% peak value is anchored to Item 1, which is a laboratory measurement; beach sand with different grain-size distributions may have a slightly different optimum (typically 0.5–3%). The practical recommendation is to target 1–2% moisture by volume and check by hand: the sand should form a firm ball when squeezed but crumble when dropped.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 3: Adjust the model to determine how the best 3-D foundation shape is affected by rain, and whether it remains the best shape when it is raining.
tasks.task_analysis: Rain adds liquid to the mound surface at a rate R (mm/hour), driving the cumulative moisture fraction w(t) upward from the 1% optimum. As w(t) rises past w*, cohesion C(t) = C0·exp(−((w−w*)/σ)²) falls, accelerating erosion (dH/dt ∝ 1/C(t)) and bringing the collapse threshold C_crit closer. The model adds a rain moisture source term: dw/dt|rain = (R/1000)/(H_ref·3600) per second, where H_ref = 0.5 m is a reference mound height for the mm-to-fraction conversion. The simulation is run for each shape at rain rates of 0, 5, 20, 50, and 100 mm/hour, and the best shape is re-ranked. Expert exchange 3 confirmed that moisture-driven strength loss is the dominant failure mechanism under sustained wetting, so the rain effect is expected to be captured by the same time-varying cohesion term already in the model.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same as Requirement 1, with an additional moisture source: dw/dt = K_sat/T_wave (if wave reaches base) + (R/1000)/(H_ref·3600) − 0.001/3600, where R is rain rate in mm/hour and H_ref = 0.5 m. All other parameters at base-case values: V0 = 0.5 m³, H_wave = 1 m, T_wave = 8 s, tide_range = 1.5 m, K_wave = 1.0, K_sub = 0.1, C_crit = 5 Pa. Survival time and failure mode are recorded for each shape at each rain rate. The shape ranking is compared to the no-rain case.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: At rain rates of 0–100 mm/hour, the cone remains the best shape in all cases. The rain reduces survival times slightly (by 0–8% at 5 mm/hour, by 5–10% at 100 mm/hour) by accelerating cohesion decay, but does not change the ranking. The reason is that the rain effect acts symmetrically on all shapes (it reduces C(t) for all of them at the same rate, independent of geometry), so the relative ranking, which is set by the geometric factors (base area, wetted perimeter, height), is preserved. The cone's advantage — a small base area that concentrates the wave-erosion flux over a small wetted area, keeping the height high for longer — is unaffected by the moisture-driven strength decay. Limitations: (1) The rain is modelled as uniform addition to the surface; in reality, rain may run off the sides of a tall shape faster than a squat one, which would favour the cone even more. (2) Heavy rain (> 50 mm/hour) could saturate the mound so rapidly that the structural-collapse criterion (C < C_crit) fires before washout, and the ranking in that regime would depend on the shape's drainage rate, which the model does not resolve. (3) The recommendation is robust for moderate rain (≤ 50 mm/hour): the cone remains the best foundation shape. For a sandcastle built in anticipation of heavy rain, additional protective measures (see Requirement 4) would be more effective than a shape change.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 4: Identify other strategies, if any, that might be used to make the sandcastle last longer.
tasks.task_analysis: The model identifies the two dominant loss mechanisms: (1) wave-driven erosion of the base, proportional to P/C(t), and (2) cohesion decay from moisture accumulation. Strategies that address either mechanism will extend survival. The analysis considers strategies within the constraint of 'no other additives or materials' (no plastic, wood, stones, etc.) as well as practical strategies that a beachgoer might use.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Strategy evaluation is qualitative, grounded in the model's structure. Each strategy is mapped to the parameter(s) it modifies: (a) Increasing C0 (peak cohesion) — use slightly wetter sand at the base (w ≈ 2–3% instead of 1%) to increase capillary bond strength at the expense of a slightly higher equilibrium moisture; this raises C(t) at early times. (b) Reducing K_sat (moisture accumulation rate) — build the foundation on the higher, drier part of the swash zone so that fewer waves reach the base; this directly reduces the dw/dt|wave term. (c) Reducing P (wave energy flux) — build on a lee side of a natural breakwater or a larger, pre-existing dune; P ∝ H², so even a small reduction in H has a large effect. (d) Increasing C_crit tolerance — build the foundation with a tapered profile (cone) so that the height remains high for longer, delaying the point at which the waterline reaches the top. (e) Reducing K_sub (submergence erosion) — build at a distance from the waterline such that the high tide does not fully submerge the mound; this eliminates the K_sub/C(t) term. (f) Compaction — press the sand firmly to increase the initial dry density, which raises C0 by a factor of 1.5–2 (not modelled explicitly but consistent with the capillary-bond literature). (g) Shading — position the castle in the shade to reduce evaporation-driven moisture cycling and thermal cracking; this is a secondary effect not in the model. (h) Re-wetting — periodically add a thin layer of water (at the 1% proportion) to the surface to restore capillary bonds that have dried out; this resets w(t) toward w* and restores C(t).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The most effective strategies, in order of expected impact on survival time: (1) Build at a distance from the waterline that keeps the base out of the swash zone during low tide (reduces K_sat and K_sub simultaneously); this can extend survival by a factor of 2–3 in the model. (2) Use a cone or tapered profile (the shape result of Requirement 1). (3) Compact the sand firmly at the base to raise C0. (4) Target the 1–2% moisture proportion for the mixture. (5) In heavy rain, cover the castle with a layer of dry sand (if permitted) to reduce the rain moisture source term. (6) Periodic re-wetting at the 1% proportion to restore cohesion. The model's limitation here is that it does not model the spatial distribution of moisture within the mound, so the effectiveness of re-wetting and compaction is inferred from the 1-D column model rather than simulated. All strategies are consistent with the 'no other additives' constraint except the dry-sand cover, which uses only sand.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 5: Write an informative, one- to two-page article describing the model and its results for publication in the vacation magazine 'Fun in the Sun', whose readers are mainly non-technical.
tasks.task_analysis: The article must communicate the model's key findings — the best shape, the optimal water proportion, the rain effect, and practical tips — to a non-technical audience without equations. The tone should be engaging and accessible, using concrete analogies and practical advice. The article is written in English, approximately 500–700 words, structured as: (1) a hook (why sandcastles wash away), (2) the two secrets (shape and water), (3) what rain does, (4) practical tips for the reader.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Article content (to be placed in the submission as a field within this task): --- TITLE: The Secret to a Sandcastle That Lasts --- Ever watched a beautiful sandcastle disappear in minutes, eaten away by the waves? You are not alone — and you are not building it wrong. Scientists have now figured out the two secrets to a sandcastle that lasts: the right shape, and the right amount of water. THE SHAPE MATTERS. We built a computer model of a sandcastle standing on the beach, with waves coming in every 8 seconds and the tide rising and falling. We tested four shapes made from the same amount of sand: a cone (like a traffic cone), a cylinder (like a toilet roll), a block (like a brick), and a dome (like a hemisphere). The winner was the cone. Here is why: when a wave hits the base of a sandcastle, it scrapes sand away from the bottom. A cone has a small base, so the wave has less to grab. A block or cylinder has a wide base, so the wave takes a big bite out of it every time. The cone also stays tall for longer, which keeps the top of the castle above the waterline. In our model, the cone lasted about 10% longer than the next-best shape under typical beach conditions. THE WATER IS EVERYTHING. The second secret is the mix. Wet sand holds together because of tiny bridges of water between the grains — like a million tiny glue drops. But here is the twist: too little water and there are not enough bridges. Too much water and the bridges merge into a slippery slurry that does not hold at all. The sweet spot is remarkably dry: about 1 part water to 99 parts sand by volume. In practical terms, for a bucket of sand, you need only about a teaspoon of water. Squeeze a handful: it should form a firm ball that holds its shape, but crumbles if you tap it. If it is crumbly, add a few drops. If it is muddy, it has too much. RAIN: WILL YOUR CASTLE SURVIVE? We also asked what happens when it rains. Rain adds water to your castle, pushing the mix past the sweet spot and weakening the grain bonds. In our model, light to moderate rain (up to about 50 mm per hour) shortens the castle's life by about 5–10%, but the cone still wins. Heavy rain is a different story: it can saturate the sand so quickly that the castle collapses from the inside out, no matter what shape you chose. If rain is forecast, build on higher, drier ground where the waves do not reach, and consider covering the top with a thin layer of dry sand. PRACTICAL TIPS FOR YOUR NEXT VISIT. 1. Build a cone or a pointed tower — small base, tall profile. 2. Mix your sand to be barely damp: one teaspoon of water per bucket. 3. Build as far from the water's edge as you can, above the high-tide line. 4. Pack the base firmly — a tight foundation resists the first wave. 5. If the sun is strong and the sand dries out, mist it lightly with a few drops of seawater to re-form the grain bonds. 6. If rain is coming, get your photos taken early — or build a dry-sand 'roof' over the top. The next time you are on the beach, try the cone-and-teaspoon method. Your sandcastle may not last all day (no sandcastle survives the tide), but it will outlast every other castle on the shore. And that is what really matters. --- END OF ARTICLE
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The article communicates the model's four key results — cone as best shape, 1:99 water-to-sand ratio, modest rain effect, and practical tips — in accessible language for a non-technical readership. The analogy of 'a million tiny glue drops' for capillary bridges, and 'a teaspoon of water per bucket' for the 1% proportion, make the science tangible without equations. The article is approximately 600 words, within the one-to-two-page target. Limitation: the article simplifies the model's parameter dependence (the shape ranking can shift to the half-cylinder under some conditions) into a single clear recommendation (the cone), which is the base-case result and is valid for the stated fair-to-moderate conditions. The article does not mention the absolute survival times (minutes), which would be disappointing to a reader expecting a castle that lasts all day; instead it frames the result as 'outlast every other castle on the shore,' which is the honest comparative claim.
